analysis.one_liner: Taxes private equity and hedge fund managers' profit shares as ordinary income instead of at lower capital gains rates.
analysis.headline: A bill from Sen. Wyden with 14 Senate cosponsors to tax investment fund managers' profit shares as ordinary income was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2026 and has sat there since with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would close the carried interest loophole, which lets managers of private equity, hedge fund, and real estate partnerships pay lower capital gains tax rates on the share of fund profits they receive as compensation for managing other people's money. It would instead tax those profit shares as ordinary income, charge managers income tax on the fair market value of a profit share when they receive it, and apply a minimum ordinary-income charge to performance-based allocations each year. It also repeals the existing three-year holding rule that only partially limited the loophole.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, especially wage earners, who already pay ordinary income tax rates on their compensation. Fund managers' profit shares are compensation for a service, and this bill would tax them on the same basis, restoring revenue to the Treasury and removing a tax advantage available almost exclusively to high-earning investment managers.

how_it_helps.text: Treats performance-based partnership interests held by investment managers as generating ordinary income up to a minimum amount set by the fund's invested capital and a statutory rate, so profit shares are taxed like work income rather than like investment gains.

Requires a manager who receives a partnership interest for services to pay tax on its fair market value at the time it is received, closing the gap between how fund managers and ordinary employees are taxed on compensation.
Repeals Section 1061 of the tax code, the three-year holding rule enacted in 2017 that left the carried interest advantage largely intact.

The definition of covered activity explicitly includes investing in securities, commodities, and real estate held for rental or investment, so the rules reach private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate fund managers rather than one industry alone, and it directs the Treasury to write anti-abuse rules against restructurings, undervaluation, and tiered entities.

analysis.who_pays: Fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate investment firms, who would pay ordinary income tax rates (top rate 37%, plus Medicare taxes) on profit shares instead of the 20% long-term capital gains rate, and who would owe a minimum charge each year based on the size of the fund they manage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: The minimum charge is based on the fund's invested capital and the manager's profit percentage rather than the manager's actual profits in that year, so a manager could owe ordinary income tax even in a year when the fund loses money.

The bill is complex: it requires partnerships to compute and report a 'deemed compensation amount' for each covered partner each year, using valuations, measurement dates, and anti-abuse rules that the Treasury would have to spell out in regulations, creating significant compliance costs.

Because it covers real estate held for rental or investment as well as securities, higher taxes on fund managers could raise the cost of capital for the companies, startups, and rental properties those funds finance — the standard objection the investment industry has raised to every carried-interest bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real inequity: income earned by managing other people's money is currently taxed at investment-gains rates even though it is compensation for a service, a break ordinary workers managing no one's money but their own cannot get. The cost falls on a small, very high-earning group. The design is blunt — the minimum charge applies based on fund size whether or not the fund profits, and the compliance burden is real — but those costs weigh against a fairness gain for everyone who pays ordinary rates on their own labor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote; the Congress does not end until January 2027, so it is not formally dead yet.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on April 16, 2026, with 13 Senate cosponsors; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, the committee that handles tax legislation.
The bill's 14 cosponsors are all Democrats and independents; no Republican signed on.
No further action has been taken: the action history shows nothing after the referral to Finance, no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, and real estate firms are better off, because the current tax treatment of their profit shares — lower capital gains rates on compensation — remains untouched. So do the clients those firms advise, at least in the short term.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 14 cosponsors; the bill was referred to the Finance Committee.

for.name: 2 of 2 Senate independents
for.role: Cosponsors (Angus King of Maine and Bernie Sanders of Vermont)

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule a hearing or markup on the bill in the months after it was referred to his committee.

against.name: 55 of 55 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, and the Republican majority took no action to bring it to the floor.

against.name: Private equity and investment fund industry groups
against.what_they_did: Have long campaigned against carried-interest tax increases, arguing they would reduce investment; the industry's past lobbying helped sink similar proposals, including one dropped from the 2017 tax law.

sides.party_line_note: Support is entirely Democratic: 12 of 45 Senate Democrats and both independents cosponsored, while none of the 55 Republicans did, and the Republican-run Finance Committee has taken no action on the bill.

industries.note: Managers' carried interest — the share of fund profits they take as compensation — would be taxed at ordinary income rates up to a minimum charge based on fund size, instead of the 20% capital gains rate. Their lower-rate tax advantage over ordinary wage earners is what the bill removes.

Performance fees would face the same ordinary-income and minimum-charge treatment, and managers selling their interest early would owe tax on years they have not yet worked under the 10-year recapture rule.
Real estate held for rental or investment is a 'specified asset', so real estate fund sponsors' profit interests are covered, closing a route that earlier carried-interest bills left open.
Venture partners' carried interest in startup funds would be taxed as compensation, which the industry argues would make it harder to raise and deploy risk capital into new companies.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no committee action since April 2026, and a Republican chair and Senate majority controlling the calendar, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or floor vote before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027. Its only realistic paths are a committee hearing if leadership chooses one, or provisions surviving inside a much larger tax bill — both long shots with the current makeup of the Senate.
